title: High Schoolers Push to Extend the Voting Age to 16 for Local Elections in This LA Suburb
author: Pascal Sabino
content:
When the Culver City Unified School District hit a budget crisis in 2025,
students say they suffered but had no say in the changes that were coming as
the school board cut millions of dollars and more than three dozen staff.

Students had two members on the board, but those seats were largely
ceremonial; while all three representatives called on the board to protect the
district’s art program and keep the schools fully staffed, the board moved
forward with the cuts.

Fed up at the decisions being made about their education without having any
real voice on the board, students have been leading a campaign to lower the
voting age for local elections in Culver City, an affluent suburb surrounded
by the city of Los Angeles.

A proposed charter amendment that Culver City students have been pushing for
years, which will be on the ballot in November as Measure YV, would allow 16-
and 17 year-olds to cast ballots for city council and the school board
elections.

Mia Moroz, a senior at Culver City High School and president of Vote 16 Culver
City, the school club that has been leading the campaign for years, says the
school board and city council have “been creating policy that alters the lives
of our teenagers without giving them a way to voice their opinion.”

Moroz says the [budget
cuts](https://culvercitycrossroads.com/2025/03/05/ccusd-approves-budget-cuts-
ends-dei-administration-position/) the board made last year, $3.4 million in
total, were done in a way that has been “deeply detrimental” for
students—including laying off 39 employees ranging from teachers to a nurse,
counselor and assistant superintendent for diversity, equity and inclusion.
Then this year came with [more layoffs](https://www.culvercrescent.com/ccusd-
approves-2026-layoff-notices/) that Moroz says fell especially hard on the
high school’s “beloved and revered” art program.

After the latest round of cuts were announced this year in March, students and
teachers [rallied](https://www.culvercrescent.com/when-the-house-is-already-
burning-ccusd-to-reconsider-counselor-cuts/) outside a local middle school to
warn that the staffing shortages and growing class sizes would shortchange the
quality of education in Culver City. “It looks like teachers who have 42 kids
in one classroom and not enough seats to sit down,” Moroz said of the recent
cuts. “And it looks like our girls’ bathroom not having soap since the first
day of school.”

Students at Culver City High School have advocated for years through the Vote
16 Culver City club for lowering the voting age. They came close in 2022, the
first time they got the city council to put a measure on the ballot, but it
[failed by just 16 votes](https://results.lavote.gov/#year=2022&election=4300)
out of the more than 16,500 cast. The club tried to run an
[initiative](https://www.c-c-d-c.com/the-case-for-letting-16-year-olds-vote-
in-culver-city-elections/) in 2024, but they couldn’t collect enough
signatures to put the item on the ballot, in part due to restrictions that
require an adult chaperone to circulate a petition.

After students renewed the campaign this year, the Culver City Council [voted
3-2 in
February](https://www.culvercityobserver.com/story/2026/02/19/news/move-to-
allow-sixteen-year-olds-to-vote-returns-again/15801.html) to put it in front
of the voters again.

Opponents of the measure call it common sense that 16-year-olds are too young
and inexperienced to weigh in on local politics. Ronald Ostrin, an attorney
who spoke against the measure at city council meetings, called students
“malleable and persuadable,” and argued that putting a ballot in their hands
would make them easy targets of political groups seeking an upper hand in
local elections.

“I’m sure there are a lot of 16-year-olds who are very mature and very
informed, the vast majority are not,” Ostrin told _Bolts._ “They haven't paid
taxes. They haven't owned property. They are easily persuadable, and so people
are attempting to gain votes through aims that are not really designed to
create an informed electorate.”

Steve Gourley, a former mayor who opposes the student voting measure, calls it
a “power grab” by the city council’s left flank that would allow them to
easily control city politics by catering to students.

“They've been changing things like crazy,” Gourley told _Bolts_ , pointing to
a [$20 million investment](https://www.culvercrescent.com/council-officially-
commits-to-jubilo-village-in-split-vote/) into an affordable housing project
last year and an earlier move to [reduce the number of sworn
officers](https://www.culvercity.gov/City-Hall/Reports-policies-local-
laws/Police-Reform/Elimination-of-Sworn-Police-Officer-Positions) in the
Culver City Police Department. Gourley argued that adding 16- and 17-year-olds
to the electorate would incentivize worse spending decisions to “appease the
students.”

“I would hate that the people running for school board would have to show up
at the rally that the students put on at the school and listen to their input
in order to become elected officials,” he said. “What if they want an extra
day off school? What if they don't want to take this course, or that one?”

Organizers behind the measure say it’s hardly a power grab, but rather the
result of years of sustained organizing from multiple cohorts of student
activists who have met regularly with city leaders, spoken at many council
meetings, canvassed their neighbors, and written [op-eds in the local
paper](https://culvercitycrossroads.com/2019/09/10/dear-editor-vote-16/) to
drum up support for the reform.

As for the accusation that 16- and 17-year-olds are too immature and
uninformed to vote in local elections, Moroz said students may actually be
more informed about government and politics than some adults because the state
requires them to study those issues in civics classes.

“I see all of these students who are so often disregarded as being immature,
or not knowledgeable, or disengaged. But I see them caring, and I see them
acting,” Moroz said.

Members of the Culver City Vote 16 club hosted a town hall at a local coffee
shop in early October where they urged community members to canvass and put up
lawn signs for Measure YV. Some who commended the student’s efforts had
previously participated in protests in the 70’s that succeeded in lowering the
voting age from 21 to 18—when, amid the Vietnam War, advocates for lowering
the age argued that teens who were old enough to fight and die for the country
were also old enough to have a voice in electing the leaders who would send
them off to battle.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/IMG_2798-2400x1600.jpg)Students with Vote 16 Culver
City hosted a local event in early October to raise support for this year's
ballot measure. (Photo courtesy of Vote 16 Culver City)

One resident at the town hall said he supported allowing students to help
elect their school board, but he couldn’t get behind allowing them to vote in
city council elections since students aren’t directly involved in many of the
issues that pass through city hall.

The idea of lowering the voting age has gradually gained traction in
California, with the Bay Area cities of Berkeley and Oakland allowing 16- and
17-year-olds to [participate in school
board](https://edsource.org/2024/berkeley-oakland-teens-cast-first-votes-in-
school-board-elections/721392) elections, but not city council elections,
since 2024.

These reforms built on earlier experiments with lowering the voting age to 16-
and 17-year-olds in Maryland, [where 10 cities and
towns](https://cdce.umd.edu/sites/cdce.umd.edu/files/Expanding%20Youth%20Suffrage_%20An%20Analysis%20of%20Vote16%20Potential%20Across%20MD%20Municipalities.pdf)
made the change for local elections, beginning in 2013 with Takoma Park, a
suburb of the nation’s capital. Newark, New Jersey, started allowing 16- and
17-year-olds to vote in  school board races [last
year](https://boltsmag.org/newark-teens-gear-up-for-school-board-elections-
after-voting-age-extended-to-16/).

Advocates say high turnout among teens observed in some of those
cities—[sometimes twice that of the general
population](https://selc.senate.ca.gov/sites/selc.senate.ca.gov/files/final-
md-case-study_generation_citizen_vote16usa.pdf)—provides a glimpse of how
Culver City may benefit from the measure, though that pattern [did not hold in
Newark](https://www.chalkbeat.org/newark/2025/05/09/less-than-four-percent-of-
teens-vote-in-2025-school-board-election/) last year. Several other countries,
including Argentina, Austria and Brazil also allow teens as young as 16 to
vote, and the United Kingdom plans to lower the voting age in the [next
general elections](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c628ep4j5kno). Supporters
attending the town hall earlier this month at the Culver City coffee shop
[touted studies on those places
suggesting](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-32541-1_2) that people who
participate in elections at an earlier age are likely to keep voting and
engaging with civic life.

“We are at an existential moment for democracy in this country. And here we
have people who are ready and willing to be engaged,” said Culver City Vice
Mayor Bubba Fish, who voted with two others on the 5-member council to put the
amendment on the November ballot. “It creates habitual voters for life. When
they start voting earlier, they keep voting.”

LaJuan Allen, the executive director of Vote 16 USA who joined the students at
the event, also argued that excluding young people from civic life trains them
to be disengaged even when they come of age. He thinks that bringing young
people into the fold at an earlier age can be a way of addressing the poor
turnout rates and disillusionment among voters.

“For us as adults to completely disregard them is the reason why trust in
American democracy among young people continues to erode,” Allen said during
the event.

Student advocates aren’t just engaging with adults. They’re also working with
their peers to build an electorate of teens informed and prepared to
participate. The Vote 16 Culver City club regularly hosts civic education
events and pre-registration drives that help get more teens automatically put
on the voting rolls once they’re eligible—something they’ve done even in years
when lowering the voting age wasn’t on the ballot.

“How better can we prepare our youth for the realities of civic and political
engagement than by including them in it? How better can we represent their
needs than by asking them what they are?” Moroz asked. “The answer is simple:
We must give them the chance to engage.”
